t: Should Welders Care About History Class — or Algebra 2? Or Literature?
q: First, we empathize. It is painful to feel that you’re being forced to do something that has no relevance or value to your life. Think about the last PD or meeting you went to that felt like this.

Any time our students say, “This is dumb,” “This is pointless,” “This is annoying,” our work as a professional begins. The professional doesn’t say, “Well fine then, this child is just unmotivated and apathetic and there’s nothing I can do.
We’ve got to become apologists for education. An apologist is a defender, an upholder, a proponent of something controversial.

In 2019, it actually is a minority worldview that an education is an inherently beautiful and unending and emancipatory thing. To say, “Well, an education’s value isn’t just what’s measured on the test, isn’t just what’s going to be useful in your job,” is to invite scoffing.
So own the reasons you became a teacher to begin with. Grapple earnestly with the gaps between what an education ought to be and what the system currently makes it out to be.

From the empathetic position — and all the great apologists work from there — engage with the concerns of your would-be welder in the British Literature class, your hopes-to-work-in-HVAC student in Chemistry. And as I often recommend when I’m speaking with teachers, come up with not only one, not only five, but twenty or more arguments for why the work you do in your class is worthy work despite its lack of direct connection to someone’s future job.

The key point with our welder friend is that the public education experiment was never meant to simply prepare people for jobs. A system just focused on that one outcome is a system that has lost its soul.
x: Respond first with empathy, remembering how it feels to be forced into work that seems pointless.
Respond first with empathy, remembering how it feels to be forced into work that seems pointless.
Teachers must become apologists for education, arguing to heart and imagination as well as to logic.
Stuart takes up a common motivational obstacle: students and parents who say a course is worthless because it does not connect to a future job.
A system that only prepares workers has lost its soul, so teachers should speak a bigger vision of education.
Prepare twenty or more arguments for why the work matters beyond job relevance.
His claim is that public education was never meant simply to prepare people for jobs and that teachers keep it from losing its soul one interaction at a time.

t: What About When Effort Doesn’t Work?
q: For our students to bring effort to the mastery work in our classes, they’ve got to believe that their effort is actually going to pay off. You and I are not so different. Why try if it won’t matter?
Normalize the failure. “Yeah, this happens. I’ve seen this before. The best thing for us to do is to sit down and look at how you studied so that we can make a plan for next time.

If the failure-despite-effort is just happening with a student or two, then I like to schedule fifteen minutes with that student to look at what kind of effort they put in. I ask lots of questions here. I ask them to show me their notes.

I keep an index card between us, and we write down things to try next time on the card (e.g., “Space the three hours of studying out over two weeks in 30-minute sessions rather than doing one giant cram at the end,” or, “Quiz yourself with flashcards of key terms instead of rereading your notes”).
If it’s a whole-class failure-despite-effort, then do the debrief with the whole class. Use Think-Pair-Share to have students write what specifically they did to prepare for the thing.

Never communicate, explicitly or otherwise, “Well, you should just try harder.” This is a vague notion that, in my observations, works for about 1% of the population. For 99% of us, high challenge and no support means long-term frustration, not long-term flourishing.
x: His starting point is that students will only invest effort if they believe it will pay off, so a failed attempt can quietly erode that belief.
Normalizing failure signals that the teacher knows what to do next, which steadies the student.
Students keep trying only if they believe effort pays off, so failure despite effort threatens the belief that sustains learning.
A fifteen-minute individual debrief about how the student actually prepared, ending with an index card of strategies to try, turns failure into a plan.
He offers a short protocol: normalize the failure, debrief individually with a student using an index card of next-time strategies, and run a Think-Pair-Share debrief when the whole class struggled.
He closes with a warning against telling students to try harder, which leaves most of them with high challenge and no support.

q: It’s behavior that isn’t dangerous or threatening, and therefore doesn’t rise to the level of involving an administrator.
The key to handling brazen behavior is to control your desire to rush in, show your displeasure, and put them in their place.
Your students will be expecting you to act shocked and angry, like most adults in similar situations. You must do the opposite.
Keeping it a mystery from the rest of the class sends a stronger message that such behavior is unacceptable.
Just review what they did, remind them of the addendum, and tell them what the consequence will be. Do not lecture or tell them what to think or how they should feel.
Brazenness shows a clear lack of respect for you, for learning, and for their fellow classmates. It will grow and spread unless you handle it with the shrewd craftiness it deserves.
x: Linsin defines 'brazen behavior' as disruptive, silly, or defiant acts—like running, yelling, or throwing objects—that fall short of requiring administrator involvement but still create a scene the whole class notices.

t: The Trait Every Great Teacher Shares
q: It’s something lasting, highly influential, and part of who the teacher is. It’s woven into their manner and demeanor.
You see, teachers who are uncertain or dubious about their classroom management approach always struggle.
Students know fear and weakness in their teacher when they see it, even if it lies below the surface. They can smell it from across the playground.
You can be confident and surefooted outside of the classroom and find yourself perplexed and struggling for air within it. Teaching can be especially unforgiving in this way.
You’re better off embracing one methodology than following your own hybrid system or an approach you don’t fully understand.
Which puts them at ease, removes their excitability, and frees them to settle down, settle in, and focus on learning.
x: Linsin identifies commitment—full, undivided commitment to one classroom management approach—as the invisible trait that separates great teachers from struggling ones.
Identifies full commitment to one classroom management approach as the key trait separating great teachers from struggling ones.
